summary: Albertus Bruining (1846–1919) was a scholar in religious studies and Indology. He studied at the University of Amsterdam and Leiden University (Dr.theol. c. 1865–1871 under Johan Hendrik Caspar Kern and Paul Deussen), becoming Professor of Theology at Amsterdam in 1900.

Albertus Wilhelmus van den Hoek (1951–2001) specialized in Indology. He studied at the University of Amsterdam and Leiden University (B.A. c. 1968–1970, M.A. c. 1970–1976 under Jan C. Heesterman, and with Louis Dumont in 1977), later serving as head at Leiden (1989–1992).
Albinas Rimka (1886–1944) worked in Indology and other fields. He taught economics at Vytautas Magnus University from 1923 to 1925 and at Vilnius University in 1940.

Albion Moonlight Butters specializes in Tibetology and Buddhist studies. He earned a B.A. at UC Santa Cruz, an M.T.S. at Harvard, and a Ph.D. at Columbia under Robert A. F. Thurman (attested 2006). He taught at the University of Turku (2013–2020).

Albrecht Hanisch is a scholar in Indology and Buddhist studies. He earned his doctorate at the University of Marburg by 2000 under Michael Hahn, later serving as Acting Director at the Nepal Research Centre and Local Representative for the Nepalese-German Manuscript Cataloguing Project.

Albrecht Weber (1825–1901) was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Breslau, Bonn, and Berlin (1842–1845) under Adolf Friedrich Stenzler, Christian Lassen, Johann Gildemeister, and Adalbert Kuhn. He held posts including adjunct professor and Privatdozent at Humboldt University of Berlin.

Albrecht Wezler (1938–2023) was an Indology and philosophy scholar. He earned his doctorate at Tübingen under Paul Thieme (c. 1960–1965) and served as Director at the University of Hamburg, the Nepal-German Manuscript Preservation Project, and the Nepal Research Centre.

Aleix Ruiz-Falqués works in Indology, Buddhist studies, and linguistics. He completed his Ph.D. at the University of Cambridge under Eivind Kahrs by 2016, and held posts at Shan State Buddhist University, Singapore University of Technology and Design, and the Pali Text Society.

Aleksander Brückner (1856–1939) was a linguist and historian who studied at the University of Lviv, the University of Vienna, and Frederick William University Berlin, learning from August Leskien. He held academic posts at the University of Lviv and Frederick William University Berlin.

Aleksander Dunin Borkowski (1811–1896) was an Indology scholar. He pursued philological studies at Chernivtsi University (1827), the University of Lviv (c. 1827–1831), and the University of Königsberg (c. 1833–1835), where he studied under Peter von Bohlen.

Aleksandr Arnol'dovich Freiman (1879–1968) was an Iranian and Central Asian studies scholar and linguist. He studied at Saint Petersburg State University and Giessen under Christian Bartholomae, Carl Salemann, Sergey Oldenburg, Fyodor Shcherbatskoy, and Jan Baudouin de Courtenay, later chairing Iranian philology at Saint Petersburg.

Aleksandr Gilferding (1831–1872) worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied under Viktor Grigorovich at Moscow State University, completing his master's dissertation in 1852–1853, and served as President of the Slavic Benevolent Society and the Russian Geographical Society.

Aleksandr Ivanovich Aleksandrov (1861–1918) was a linguist who studied at Kazan State University under Jan Niecisław Baudouin de Courtenay and Mikołaj Kruszewski, and at Tartu. He was Professor of Comparative Linguistics and Sanskrit at Kharkiv and later at Kazan State University.

Aleksandr Ivanovich Tomson (1864–1935) was a linguist. He studied at Saint Petersburg State University (1882–1887) under Filipp Fedorovich Fortunatov and Theodor Korsch, and served as ordinary Professor of Indo-European Linguistics and Sanskrit at Odesa University from 1897 to 1932.

Aleksandr Leonovič Grjunberg-Cvetinovič (1930–1995) was a scholar of linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology. He studied at Saint Petersburg State University under Ivan Ivanovich Zarubin and held longtime posts at the university and the Institute of Linguistic Studies.

Aleksandr Lvovich Duvernois (1840–1886) was a linguist who studied at Moscow State University from 1855 to 1866 under Pavel Jakovlevič Petrov. He later served as Professor of Comparative Linguistics at Moscow State University from c. 1869 to 1886.

Aleksandr Mervart (1884–1932) specialized in Indology and linguistics. He earned his Ph.D. at Heidelberg University (c. 1904–1907), taught at Saint Petersburg State University (1924–1930), and served as head of the Indian Department and Keeper at the Kunstkamera.

Aleksandr Mikhailovich Osipov (1897–1969) worked in Indology and history/archaeology. After studying at Moscow State University (c. 1920–1926), he taught at the Moscow Institute of Oriental Studies, worked at the International Agrarian Institute, and held the Indian History chair at Moscow State University.

Aleksandr Semënovič Zimin (1880–1942) was an Indologist who studied under Fyodor Shcherbatskoy in 1920. He served as a Docent at the Leningrad Oriental Institute starting in 1934 and held a post at the Institute of Oriental Manuscripts in 1937.

Aleksandr Vasil'yevich Popov (1855–1880) was a scholar in Indology and linguistics. He attended the Kupiansk Theological Seminary from 1871 to 1875 and studied under Vincenz Scherzl from c. 1874 to 1879.
